rv.q: Producers and creatives have smartly crafted a polished production for this revival — but in a competitive Broadway season, the show may need some luck, and the critics’ blessings, to ensure it survives longer than the musical’s first visit to the Rialto.
All the parts are good. They just, maddeningly, don't add for a stunning show.

This new version of 'Gigi' feels like a musical in the witness protection program, disguised beyond ready recognition.
This is some very flat champagne.

The attempt to turn such a property into a girl-power fantasy, in part by casting Disney star Vanessa Hudgens as Gigi — and in part by de-perving it completely — has left it more perverted than ever, and altogether unworthy of its name.
Whatever good work Thomas was doing to save "Gigi" from its previous self is undermined by the central performance, which is all at sea even before you ponder the vocal limitations thereof.
Every moment Hudgens isn’t onstage, you long for her return—not only for her dramatic talents, but also because she wears Catherine Zuber’s beautiful costumes so breathtakingly well.

But it's lovingly updated in a new Broadway incarnation directed by Eric Schaeffer, with magnificent visuals of Belle Epoque Paris, arresting choreography and, yes, a charming performance by leading lady Vanessa Hudgens.
Indeed, they’re as tedious for us to watch as Gigi claims they are.
Ironically, though, Gaston's courtship of Gigi comes across as creepier here than it did when a thirtysomething Louis Jourdan pursued a dewy Leslie Caron (then Hudgens' age) onscreen.
This Gigi is gorgeous to look at and boasts a fine performance from Vanessa Hudgens in the title role, but it's dramatically inert and musically disappointing.
When all is said and done, Gigi is an insubstantial property, despite a peerless score by Lerner and Loewe.
Otherwise, 'Gigi' is the night the Champagne went flat.
If it comes to that, this whole Gigi is lacking in charm, if not nerve.
Hudgens gives the sort of sincere but clumsy performance you’d expect to see in, well, a high school musical.
Yet the new revival of Gigi too often feels akin to dirty linen that’s been put through the wash too many times; it’s clean now and has a sheen, but it’s threadbare, intellectually and emotionally.
The result, however, is a bland soufflé that is too hard on the outside and too soft at the center.
